extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, graduate students, and advanced creative writers studying narrative theory (Genette's narrative temporality)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how a narrative handles time: its omissions (ellipses), the distinction and function of scene vs. summary, and the relations of frequency (singulative, iterative, repeating) between narrated events and narrative statements. Useful for close reading, narrative analysis, and informed creative writing decisions about pacing and repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing ellipses (explicitly announced ellipses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses that are announced in the text and that function to characterize a period or phase (a 'negative characterization' is still a characterization). Example: Fielding's announced leap of twelve years in Tom Jones; Proust's ellipses framing the episode of the war where we learn retrospectively what Marcel did during those years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat announced ellipses as intentional characterizing devices: they both omit and comment on the omitted period. When analyzing or composing, note what is being characterized by the omission (e.g., a period of 'divine happiness', clinical convalescence, detachment) and how that characterization affects reader inference and the narrative's thematic shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit ellipses (unannounced temporal gaps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses whose presence is not signaled in the text and which readers infer from chronological lacunae or discontinuities (e.g., gaps between chapters or changes of location/apartment). Example: the indeterminate interval between chapters of Guermantes where Marcel moves apartments; the few months after the grandmother's death that remain mute and are never characterized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit ellipses demand hermeneutic attention to their duration, intensity, and placement: interpret silence (what is left out) as potentially significant. In composition, use implicit ellipses to create opacity or reticence; in analysis, account for what the silence implies about character, authorial reticence, or autobiographical transposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely hypothetical ellipses (non-localizable ellipses revealed by analepsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses impossible to localize in the narrative timeline, revealed only after the fact by analeptic reports (e.g., trips, military service). These occur at the limits of narrative coherence and temporal analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these ellipses as indicating the limits of temporal analysis; they may signal that the work deliberately transcends ordinary temporal criteria. In critical work, note that such ellipses complicate attempts to map story-time to discourse-time and may justify treating parts of the text as beyond standard temporal metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (temporal sense) redefined in Proustian narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene, taken temporally, becomes dominant in Proust insofar as ellipses are a tiny fraction of text; but Proustian scenes often are not dramatic concentrations free of digression. Instead they are 'typical or illustrative' scenes where action is often subordinated to psychological and social characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or writing, distinguish between classical dramatic scenes (focused action) and Proustian scenes (paradigmatic gatherings overloaded with commentary). Evaluate scenes not only by plot action but by their role in characterization, typification, and thematic paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inaugural/typical scene function (scene as paradigmatic representative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Long Proustian scenes often have 'inaugural' importance: each marks a hero's entrance into a milieu and stands for the entire series of similar, unreported gatherings that follow. The scene's importance comes from being first and eliciting curiosity rather than from unique dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess scenes for their inaugurative/paradigmatic role: does a scene represent an entire class of events? In composition, use an inaugural scene to open a series and to justify later elisions; in analysis, trace how initial scenes set patterns that later repetitions or elisions rely upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as 'temporal hearth' (inflation with digressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proustian scenes act as magnets for digressions—retrospections, anticipations, iterative/descriptive parentheses, narrator's didactic interventions—collecting a cluster of supplementary information around a social gathering or event (the 'supernourishment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitatively and qualitatively assess the ratio of 'external' digressive material to strictly narrative moments within scenes (examples cited: Villeparisis matinee 25/75; Guermantes dinner 43/90). In creative practice, deliberately inflate scenes with thematic digressions to make them paradigmatic; in analysis, measure how digressions change the scene's temporal texture and narrative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional summary/scene alternation and its modification
rubrics_metrics.description: In classical novelistic narrative, tempo contrast between scene and summary often mirrors content contrast (dramatic vs nondramatic); Proust modifies this: nondramatic and dramatic functions are reorganized so that the rhythmic system of the novel is profoundly affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For analysis, do not assume summary=weak content and scene=dramatic content; map how tempo choices serve different functions in modernist narratives. For writers, consider subverting conventional alternation to foreground psychological or typological material instead of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative frequency taxonomy — singulative (INlS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Singulative narrative: narrating once what happened once (the standard/default form). Genette calls this 'singulative' or 'singular' narrative (e.g., 'Yesterday, I went to bed early').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the singulative mode for discrete, non-repetitive events. In analysis, identify singulative passages as units of unique occurrence; in pedagogy, contrast them with iterative/repeating forms to show aspectual choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating n times what happened n times (nN/nS — anaphoric singulative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrating n times what happened n times (e.g., listing each day's event) is formally a repetition but is treated as singulative in Genette's grid because narrative repetitions correspond iconically to story repetitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When events and narrative statements align in count, interpret them as singulative-type treatments. Note that frequency equivalence can be stylistically mundane or used for particular effects (ritual, chronology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeating narrative (nNIlS — narrating n times what happened once)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative form where the same event is recounted multiple times in the text (e.g., recurrence of an episode told repeatedly or told from different viewpoints). Examples: the centipede death in La Jalousie; Rashomon-like point-of-view retellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify uses of repetition for perspective shifts, emphasis, or thematic recursion. In creative practice, repeat an event to explore subjectivity, variant perception, or to build mythic resonance; in analysis, track how repeated retellings change the event's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative narrative (1NlnS — narrating once what happened n times)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative narrative synthesizes multiple analogous occurrences into a single narrative utterance (e.g., 'every day' formulations). Grammatically tied to imperfect/frequentative aspect; traditionally subordinate to singulative narrative but in Proust becomes thematically and technically dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iteration to compress duration, create habitual or ritual texture, or to produce descriptive accumulation (moral portrait). In analysis, identify iterative passages and distinguish their function (background, descriptive, autonomous). Note iterative's potential to become an autonomous mode rather than mere subordinate frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: External/generalizing iteration (iterative within a scene opening to external period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative parentheses that extend beyond the scene's temporal field and 'open a window' on a wider external period (generalizing iterations). Example: at a dinner, a parenthesis summarizing months/years of relation between characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis, mark iterations that generalize beyond the immediate scene and consider how they synthesize longer temporal spans. In composition, use external iteration to provide background and to link a scene to broader social or historical patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal/synthesizing iteration (iteration over the scene itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative syllepsis that synthesizes occurrences within the temporal bounds of the scene itself (e.g., 'each time that X looked at Y... every other minute the same question seemed to be being intensely put').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when iteration functions to compress or paradigmatize events that occur within a single scene; this produces a stylized enumeration rather than a diachronic unfolding. Use internal iteration to render texture and rhythm inside scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contamination/blending of singulative scene and iteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Singulative scenes can contain iterative passages (internal or external), sometimes blending to the point that demarcation is impossible; this confuses boundaries between the single event and series it may inaugurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing, look for shifts between singulative diction and iterative formulations and consider their effects on temporal coherence and typification. For writers, blending modes can create ambiguity of scope and a sense that a single event both stands alone and symbolizes a series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-iterative (scenes presented as iterative but singular in reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rhetorical convention where scenes are worded in an iterative/imperfect tense to suggest repetition though readers understand them figuratively as single or variant instances (e.g., 'not once but a hundred times' as hyperbole). In classical narrative this is a figurative trope; in Proust this pseudo-iterative tendency becomes extensive and often intended to be taken literally—an 'intoxication with the iterative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pseudo-iteration from genuine iteration: ask whether the text intends literal repetition or figurative typification. In critical readings, note Proustian slips of tense as evidence of the author's enfolding of singulative intensity into iterative form; in creative use, pseudo-iteration can create ritualized tone or rhetorical exaggeration, but risks confusion if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative autonomy and prevalence (measure of iterative vs singulative share)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a text relies on iterative mode (e.g., Genette's approximate counts: Combray ~86 iterative to 52 singulative pages; other sections likewise) — showing that Proust's first sections are essentially iterative and that iterative can dominate structuring of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For textual analysis, quantitatively estimate iterative vs singulative proportions to show modality dominance; for composition, deliberately choose whether iterative texture will be subordinate background or an autonomous organizing principle of the work. Use counts cautiously—Genette warns against false precision—but use them to indicate tendencies.
